source.title: The Zero Pattern of a Design Matrix Drives Multiple Descent in Over-parameterized Regression
source.authors: Kevin Han Huang; Haoyu Ye; Somak Laha; Morgane Austern

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present; no material truncation or garbling noted.
record.tranche_reason: Tests double and multiple descent in over-parameterized linear regression, a different model class and design from the deep-network claim.
record.gate_note: The paper's own risk sweeps and simulations bear on double or multiple descent. Theoretical equations and cited results are not separate empirical rows. Noise and ridge regularization are not varied to test the noise/regularization version.
record.test_reason: The study tests double and multiple descent in vanishing-ridge linear regression, outside deep networks. It reports simulated and real-data risk curves against p/n, with peaks at thresholds its theory predicts. These bear on V4 (a second descent in a non-deep model class) and on V6's claim that the peak can split into several. One experiment (Figure 6) varies n with p fixed, which bears on V3. Noise and ridge strength are never varied.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is largely right. The authors conclude that rank degeneracy (zero patterns), whether from heterogeneity or dependence such as augmentation, can produce multiple risk peaks in vanishing-ridge regression. The peak locations follow a matching (Dulmage–Mendelsohn) rule. For positive-definite designs they conjecture a single peak at p/n=1, supported only by simulation. Results hold for a vanishing ridge, not the exact ridgeless interpolator.
record.recipe_differences: Linear regression with vanishing ridge and risk sweeps over p/n, heterogeneous/dependent designs, and synthetic or real data; not the original deep-network settings or method.
record.method_sensitivity: Risk peak count and locations vary with covariance support and overlap (including rho); near-zero rather than zero eigenvalues soften peaks. The augmentation block size also distinguishes augmented conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: Peak count and locations are fixed by maximum matchings and the Dulmage–Mendelsohn structure of the variance profile's zero pattern.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In linear regression, the number and locations of risk peaks are determined by where the design's covariance support loses structural rank.

record.problems: Exact ridgeless risk is not established; the analysis uses a vanishing ridge. Several empirical values are shown only in plots. The positive-definite claim is presented as a conjecture supported by simulations, not a proved result. The real/generated-data experiment is stated not to be an exact instance of the analyzed models.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix Figures E.5 and E.7 are represented by R30; their individual plotted sweep outcomes were not transcribed because the accompanying text does not state them separately. Other per-curve values in the appendix plots are not transcribed where the prose only summarizes their family-level outcome.

untested.parts: Deep networks are not studied; all models are linear regression.
Only one real/generated pooled experiment varies n. Sample counts at the peaks are not given numerically.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested across size, epochs and samples. The matching rule locates peaks along p/n only.
Label-noise level and ridge strength are not varied. Removal of the peak by optimal regularization is only cited (ref 46), not tested.

record.verdict_notes: The reader marked V6 untested. But multiple-peak splitting is a central result, so V6 is tested in part; only its noise and regularization parts are untested. R25 varies n, not capacity, so it is relinked from V4 to V3/V6. Most empirical values are figure-only. Neither original source is this study.

versions.untested_parts: Deep-network model-size scaling is not tested; the study concerns linear regression.
The real/generated-data experiment varies training-set size and reports risk peaks, but does not isolate a single peak or give numerical before/after sample-count comparisons.
Tests over-parameterized linear regression, not a broad comparison across model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested across size, epochs, and sample-count axes.
Noise level and ridge regularization are not experimentally varied. Optimal regularization is mentioned only in discussion of cited work.
The study does not recount complexity using an effective number of parameters or test whether that makes the curve an ordinary U-shape.

tranche.reason: The study investigates double and multiple descent using vanishing-ridge linear regression, variance-profile theory, and synthetic and pooled-data experiments.

source_check.notes: Theory concerns vanishing ridge, not exact zero ridge; optimal peak removal is untested. Figure E.10 is internally inconsistent: its full-rank description accompanies size = sigma = 0 and a covariance containing sigma squared.

statements.correction: Rank-deficient heterogeneous designs have shifted or multiple variance peaks determined by covariance support. Section 6.1 predicts a stationary peak at p/n = 10/9 and a moving peak; they coincide at rho = 0.35. These results extend the single-peak picture while retaining subsequent descent.
statements.problem: The structural findings are correct, but shifted or multiple peaks do not by themselves limit V4's stated claim of renewed improvement beyond interpolation. V4 does not require raw p/n = 1.
